title: An army on the shore
hookLine: the war book opens with an embrace, a march, and God in human form awake by the sea
carry: an avatar weeps: God took on a human heart

cards: The war book doesn't open with a war. It opens with a thank-you. Rama turns to Hanuman and tries to say what he's done: crossed an ocean, found her, come back.

Then Rama looks at himself: an exile in bark clothes, living on a mountain, with no kingdom, no treasury, no land to give. So he says the one gift he has left is this, and he takes Hanuman in his arms.

teach.h: HOW WILL WE ALL GET ACROSS?
teach.b: Then the thank-you turns into a question. Hanuman crossed the ocean by leaping. An army can't leap.
How will all of us get across? Sugriva answers like a good friend in a crisis: grief makes a person slow; let's march, and find the way when we're there.

So the army pours south over hills and forests, Hanuman carrying Rama on his shoulders at times, and makes camp on the last shore of the land. In front of them, the ocean, roaring, with no far shore in sight.
He speaks to the wind: you blow where she is. Touch her, and then come and touch me. Now remember who Rama is, for Hindus.
He's an avatar: Vishnu himself, come down to earth. And look at what the avatar does. He grieves.
He can't sleep. He doesn't know the way across, and he leans on a friend. That isn't a flaw in the story; it's the teaching.
Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama, the best of men, living within limits.

teach.h: GOD TOOK ON A HUMAN HEART.
teach.b: In this avatar, God doesn't skip the human part. He keeps his word, he loves, he weeps, he asks for help. Many teachers say that's why people love Rama so much: he knows a long night by the water from the inside.

how: Many Hindu homes and temples keep an image of Rama's court, the Ram darbar, with Hanuman kneeling at Rama's feet, and teachers call Rama maryada purushottama: God living a human life within its limits.

s: the Yuddha Kanda opens with a battle
it opens with Rama embracing Hanuman, the only gift he says he has.
for Hindus, Rama is an avatar of Vishnu
God come down to earth, living a fully human life.
because Rama is God, he never grieves or doubts
he can't sleep by the sea and asks the wind to touch Sita; the avatar takes on the human part too.

games.q: your little cousin asks: if Rama is God, why does he cry on the beach and not know how to cross? by the story, what's the best answer?
o: it's a mistake in the story; God can't be sad.
as an avatar, God takes on a real human life, tears and limits included.
he was only pretending, to fool Ravana's spies.
games.why: Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama: in this avatar, Vishnu lives within human limits, and his grief by the sea is part of that.

practice: Many Hindu homes keep a picture of Rama's court, the Ram darbar, with Hanuman kneeling at Rama's feet. Bring that picture to mind, or Rama holding Hanuman close.

Then bring up one thing you're grieving or worried about right now, honestly, the way Rama spoke to the wind. If you pray, tell it to Rama, who knows that night. If you don't, just let it be named, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: The bridge. Setu in Sanskrit. Before there's a single stone, there's an army on a beach, and God in human form, awake by the water, asking how they'll all get across.

orig.note: Sanskrit setu: a bridge or causeway, also a dike or boundary.

carryVoice: Your line: an avatar weeps, God took on a human heart. Tomorrow, Rama asks the ocean itself. See you tomorrow.
